Wall Street economists expected a January rise in non-farm payrolls of 237,000 and a jobless rate of 5.2 percent. They also had forecast a 0.2 percent rise in January average hourly earnings and an average workweek of 34.6 hours.
The non-farm payroll data are based on a survey of employers and the jobless rate is based on a survey of households.
The household survey also indicated that January employment rose 433,000, that the labor force grew by 509,000, and the number of unemployed rose 75,000.
The department said that starting with the January report new revisions have been introduced for the household survey, which is used to calculate the unemployment rate.
The revisions primarily reflect improved information on the demographic characteristics of immigrants to, and emigrants from, the United States.
However, Katharine Abraham, commissioner of the department's Bureau of Labor Statistics, said the unemployment rate was not affected by the revision.
Concerning the payrolls report, Abraham said bad weather affected growth in various industries, in some cases exaggerating jobs growth and in others dampening it.
But she said the factors roughly offset each other in the overall payroll estimate.
"The net effect of all of these special factors on aggregate payroll growth was small, although estimates for specific industries may be somewhat over- or understated," Abraham said.

The Labor official said the seven-tenths of an hour decline in average weekly hours in January reflected unusually harsh weather conditions. She said the decline was spread throughout major industries, with an especially large decline in construction.
